extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, judges, and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards on when the doctrine of equivalents may be applied in patent infringement, including limits (dedication by disclosure, foreseeability, prosecution history estoppel) and available remedies for disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedication by disclosure (disclosed but unclaimed subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who discloses subject matter in the specification but does not claim it cannot invoke the doctrine of equivalents to extend claim scope to encompass that disclosed-but-unclaimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court holds that Johnston, having disclosed steel substrates but limited claims to aluminum, cannot assert the doctrine of equivalents to cover the disclosed but unclaimed steel. To the extent prior cases (e.g., YBM Magnex) conflict with this holding they are overruled. The opinion treats such disclosure-as-dedication as a bar to equivalence absent other saving principles (e.g., foreseeability exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for inadvertently failing to claim disclosed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patentee inadvertently fails to claim disclosed subject matter, statutory remedies exist: filing a reissue application under 35 U.S.C. § 251 within two years of grant, or filing a separate application as a continuation under 35 U.S.C. § 120 (if timely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion notes these remedies explicitly and observes Johnston utilized continuation applications (resulting in patents cited) to obtain literal claims to the previously unclaimed subject matter. The doctrine of equivalents should not duplicate these statutory correction mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability bar to the doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents does not capture subject matter that the patent drafter reasonably could have foreseen during the application process and included in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle enhances the notice function of claims by making them the sole definition of invention scope in all foreseeable circumstances. If a person of ordinary skill would reasonably anticipate ways to evade literal claim language, the applicant has an obligation to claim those foreseeable variants; DOE will not rescue a drafter who failed to provide such notice. The court cites Sage, Maxwell, and other precedent to support this bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOE protects only insubstantial and unforeseeable equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents is meant to protect inventors from unscrupulous copyists who employ insubstantial or unanticipated variations to appropriate the claimed invention, not to allow patentees to recapture foreseeable or claimed-by-disclosure subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between protective function (preventing piracy) and notice function (defining public boundaries) requires limiting DOE to unforeseeable, insubstantial variations. The opinion references Graver Tank and Warner–Jenkinson to explain this balancing and to justify limits on DOE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-by-element requirement for applying DOE
rubrics_metrics.description: Pennwalt and Warner–Jenkinson require an equivalent for each and every element of a claim; applying DOE to the claim as a whole gives too much room to expand claim scope beyond notice limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court reiterates that DOE must be applied on an element-by-element basis rather than allowing a holistic expansion that would undermine the claim's public-notice role. Citation: Pennwalt Corp. v. Durand–Wayland and Warner–Jenkinson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel limits DOE
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history estoppel can bar a patentee from relying on non-textual infringement when subject matter was surrendered during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion explains that when a variation was neither copied nor unforeseeable at the time of filing, prosecution history estoppel may preclude DOE. The court discusses cases (e.g., Maxwell, Sage) where prosecution history affected DOE availability and emphasizes estoppel as a separate restraint on equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Festo/Warner–Jenkinson principle on surrendered subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Festo and Warner–Jenkinson propose to bar patentees from expanding their claim scope to embrace subject matter surrendered during patent acquisition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These precedents support the proposition that the public notice function requires limiting DOE when the patentee has given up claim scope during prosecution; the opinion cites Festo and Warner–Jenkinson as part of the doctrinal context limiting non-textual infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wilson Sporting Goods rule: DOE cannot embrace prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents cannot be used to expand claim scope so as to encompass the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilson Sporting Goods prevents DOE from effectively re-claiming what is in the prior art; the opinion cites Wilson as another constraint protecting the public from overbroad equivalence that would eliminate prior-art boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to foreseeability bar (after-arising technology; subtlety/complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter arising from later-developed (after-arising) technology, or subject matter cloaked by subtlety of language or complexity of the technology, may not have been foreseeable and thus may remain eligible for DOE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court recognizes that foreseeability is not absolute: after-arising technologies (Al Site, Pennwalt, Hughes Aircraft examples) and cases where the specification is complicated or claims ambiguous may permit broader indulgence. Sage and other cases are discussed as acknowledging these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-drafting obligation and premium on adequate claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applicants have an obligation to draft claims that capture all reasonably foreseeable ways to practice the invention; failure to do so places the cost on the patentee rather than the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreseeability motivates a premium on careful claim drafting; if the patentee had a clear opportunity to seek broader claims but did not, courts may bar DOE relief and expect patentees to use statutory routes (reissue/continuation) to correct claiming errors. The Sage excerpt explicitly frames this allocation of cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreseeability is an objective standard but often a factual question
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreseeability sets an objective standard for assessing when to apply DOE, but determining what was foreseeable often requires factual findings and expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurring opinions warn that foreseeability may be difficult to resolve at summary judgment because it often involves factual disputes (what one skilled in the art would have foreseen). The concurrence also notes potential overlap or tension between foreseeability and obviousness doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graver Tank distinction: claimed equivalents vs disclosed-only equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee actually claimed the equivalent subject matter (even if those claims were later held invalid), the patentee may not be treated as having dedicated that subject matter to the public; dedication-by-disclosure is a distinct concept and was not decided by Graver Tank II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The concurrence explains Graver Tank II may be distinguishable because the patentee there arguably claimed the equivalent subject matter; dedication by disclosure was not clearly decided by that Supreme Court case, so the distinction matters when assessing whether DOE is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents should not duplicate statutory correction mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of equivalents need not (and should not) duplicate the Patent Act’s statutory mechanisms for correcting claiming errors (e.g., reissue under 35 U.S.C. § 251).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion stresses that Congress provided statutory means to correct over- or under-claiming; courts should not permit DOE to substitute for those procedures, which include reissue and continuation practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-way-result (FWR) equivalence test (frequent rubric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalence is commonly assessed by whether the accused product or process performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to obtain the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One concurrence references the frequent rubric requiring substantially the same function, way, and result as a touchstone for equivalence analysis; courts must reconcile this test with foreseeability, prosecution history estoppel, and notice concerns.
